lesson.title: Menschen: wir, die Schule, der Gast, die Gruppe, der Held
lesson.subtitle: we, school, guest, group, hero — and the ancient word that means stranger and friend

hook.title: The Guest, the Group, and the Hero English Lost
hook.content: wir is the only new pronoun the A1 shelf adds: ich, du, er, sie, es — wir. It is English we with one letter moved, and it has been the same word since before either language existed. die Schule and school are the same purchase from Rome: Latin schola, from Greek scholē — a word that first meant 'leisure', the time held free for learning. der Gast is the gorgeous one: guest and Gast are the same Proto-Germanic word, and the family goes back to an ancient Indo-European word for 'stranger' that Latin adopted as hostis — whence English hostile. The stranger at your door is either the guest you welcome or the enemy you fight; one root, both futures. die Gruppe is a newer, lighter purchase: French groupe, probably from Italian gruppo, 'knot, bunch' — English bought the same French word as group. And der Held is the word English lost: Held and Old English hæleþ, 'man, warrior', are one and the same word — Germany kept it, England let it die and had to borrow Greek hērōs as hero. The hero of the German lesson is not a loan at all; it is the native Germanic champion that English still misses.

footnotes.title: One Root, Three Doors
footnotes.content: The ancient root behind Gast and guest — *ghos-ti-, 'stranger' — opened three doors. Germanic walked through one and got Gast/guest. Latin walked through another and got hostis, 'stranger, enemy', which became English hostile — and its other form hospes, 'the one who receives', became hospitable. Guest, hostile, hospitable: the same stranger, welcomed or fought.

pattern.title: Talking About the People
pattern.content: 1. wir works like every pronoun: Wir wohnen in Deutschland, Wir tanzen auf der Party. 2. The people own their verbs: Der Polizist kennt den Gast, Der Fahrer bringt den Gast, Der Kellner bringt dem Gast das Essen — the -er words from the Berufe lessons all gather here. 3. The collective takes a singular verb: Die Gruppe malt, Die Gruppe macht einen Ausflug. 4. The school frames: Die Schüler sind in der Schule, Nach der Schule ist Freizeit. 5. The stories: Der Gast kommt aus dem Dorf, Der Held mit der Gitarre, Schach mit dem Gast.
pattern.linguist_note: Schule is the Greek idea of learning-as-leisure wearing a Roman coat: scholē meant the free time a Greek citizen owned, then the lecture he filled it with, then the room he filled it in. English and German both bought the Roman word whole. The native Germanic alternative was to say it straight — die Freizeit, free time — which is exactly what the last lesson built.

exercises.target_answer: Wir wohnen in Deutschland, Die Gruppe macht einen Ausflug, Der Student in der Gruppe, Der Fahrer bringt den Gast, Der Kellner bringt dem Gast das Essen, Schach mit dem Gast, Der Gast an der Klingel, Das Butterbrot mit Marmelade für die Schule, Der Held ist Pilot, Die Gruppe ist bunt, Der Gast spricht Englisch, der Kellner Französisch und Spanisch, Der Pass und das Gepäck vom Gast
exercises.meaning: guest, group, school, hero — and the whole cast
exercises.explanation: The whole course shows up here: the jobs from the Berufe lessons, the travel words from the Reisen lessons, the party from the last one. der Gast stands at the center — the guest is who all these people work for.

exercises.prompt: One of these four wears the TH→D badge — German d where English keeps th (Dorn/thorn, der/the). Which?
exercises.meaning: das Dorf ↔ thorp: the TH→D family
exercises.explanation: das Dorf is English thorp — a word English kept only in place names, every -thorpe on the map. der Held wears the same badge against Old English hæleþ. Schule, Gast and Gruppe are loans, not shift words.

exercises.prompt: 'der Gast' and its English twin are the same Proto-Germanic word — and Latin borrowed the same root as hostis, 'enemy'. Give the English twin:
exercises.meaning: der Gast ↔ guest — and the same root gave hostile
exercises.explanation: guest and Gast are one word. The deeper aha: the ancient root meant 'stranger', and Latin turned it into hostis, enemy — whence hostile. The guest and the enemy are the same person, depending on the door.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the hero's sentence: 'The hero with the guitar'
exercises.explanation: der Held is the Old English hæleþ that English lost — Germany kept the native hero-word. And the hero, naturally, holds the Gitarre from the last lesson.
exercises.affirmation: Held was here before hero — English just forgot.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the after-school sentence: 'After school there is free time'
exercises.meaning: After school there is free time
exercises.explanation: nach + dative: nach der Schule. The sentence closes a loop — the Schule from this lesson hands the day over to the Freizeit from the last one.

summary.outcome: Speak about us and the people around you — wir, die Schule, der Gast, die Gruppe, der Held — with the whole cast of the Berufe and Reisen lessons.

use_example.german: Wir wohnen in Deutschland, und der Gast kommt aus England.
use_example.english: We live in Germany, and the guest comes from England.

summary.takeaway: wir is we, der Gast and guest share a root with hostile, der Held is the Old English hæleþ English lost — and das Dorf wears the TH→D badge as thorp.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the feelings — die Liebe, nett, wütend, stolz, die Freude: love, nice, fury, pride and joy.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Menschen: wir, die Schule, der Gast, die Gruppe, der Held (After school there is free time):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Nach der Schule ist Freizeit" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Menschen: wir, die Schule, der Gast, die Gruppe, der Held without relying on short-term echo.

wir.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wīz — the very same pronoun as English we. [wiktionary]

schule.context_phrase: Die Schule beginnt um acht Uhr.
schule.etymology_derivation: From Latin (ultimately Greek scholē) — the same classical loan as English school; see Schüler. [wiktionary]

gast.context_phrase: Wir haben heute Gäste zum Essen.
gast.context_translation: We have guests for dinner today.
gast.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *gastiz, the exact twin of English guest; Latin hostis, enemy, shows the older guest-host pair. [wiktionary]

gruppe.context_phrase: Unsere Gruppe trifft sich um acht.
gruppe.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French groupe, from Italian gruppo, ultimately from Germanic *kruppaz, lump — the same Romance round-trip word as English group. [wiktionary]

held.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *haliþ, hero, cognate with Old English hæleþ, a relative of the English health and hale family; the final th hardened to d. [wiktionary]

dorf.context_phrase: Das Dorf liegt hinter dem Berg.
dorf.context_translation: The village lies behind the mountain.
dorf.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *thurpa — Old English thorp, which survives in English place names like Mablethorpe; the English th hardened into German d. [wiktionary]

ausflug.context_phrase: Wir machen einen Ausflug in die Berge.
ausflug.context_translation: We take a trip to the mountains.
ausflug.etymology_derivation: aus (out) + Flug (flight, from fliegen — English fly): literally an out-flight, an excursion. [wiktionary]

tourist.context_phrase: Der Tourist fragt nach dem Weg.
tourist.context_translation: The tourist asks for the way.
tourist.etymology_derivation: Tour (tour, turn) + -ist; the page says it was formed in the 18th century, possibly influenced by English tourist being made at the same time from the same French material. [wiktionary]

deutschland.etymology_derivation: diutsch "of the people" + lant "land" — compound: land of the people. [wiktionary]

england.etymology_derivation: From Old English Engla land — land of the Angles. [wiktionary]

polizist.context_phrase: Der Polizist fragt nach dem Weg.
polizist.context_translation: The policeman asks about the way.
polizist.etymology_derivation: Polizei + -ist, from Greek pólis via Latin polītīa — the same loan both languages share. [wiktionary]

schüler.etymology_derivation: From Medieval Latin scholaris — the same Latin loan that gave English scholar. [wiktionary]

student.etymology_derivation: From Medieval Latin studēns — a Latin loan both languages borrowed alike. [wiktionary]

fahrer.etymology_derivation: Agent noun of fahren (to fare/drive) + -er — the fare family again. [wiktionary]

kellner.etymology_derivation: From Medieval Latin cellenarius (cellarer), from Late Latin cellarium - the pantry word that also gave German Keller and English cellar. [wiktionary][etymonline]

bäcker.etymology_derivation: Agent noun of backen (bake) + -er, Proto-Germanic *bakārijaz — the direct twin of English baker. [wiktionary]

malen.etymology_derivation: From Mal 'spot, mark'; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

party.etymology_derivation: Unadapted borrowing from English party — a doublet of older loans Partei/Partie. [wiktionary]

gitarre.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Spanish guitarra, from Arabic qithara, from Greek kithara - the same Spanish word that gave English guitar. [wiktionary]

schach.etymology_derivation: From Arabic shah, from Persian shah (king) - the same word that gave English check and checkmate (Persian shah mat, the king is dead). [wiktionary][etymonline]

freizeit.context_phrase: In meiner Freizeit lese ich Bücher.
freizeit.context_translation: In my free time I read books.
freizeit.etymology_derivation: frei + Zeit, literally free time; frei is the exact twin of free and Zeit the twin of time (as in tide, t to z). [wiktionary]

arbeiter.context_phrase: Der Arbeiter kommt um sieben Uhr.
arbeiter.context_translation: The worker comes at seven o'clock.
arbeiter.etymology_derivation: Agent noun of arbeiten (work) + -er; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

ingenieur.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French ingénieur — the same French loan as English engineer. [wiktionary]

reiten.context_translation: The child is learning to ride.
reiten.etymology_derivation: Class 1 strong verb from Proto-Germanic *rīdaną - the exact twin of English ride: reiten-ritt-geritten matches ride-rode-ridden. [wiktionary]

klingel.context_phrase: Die Klingel läutet an der Tür.
klingel.context_translation: The doorbell is ringing at the door.
klingel.etymology_derivation: From the verb klingen, meaning to ring or sound; the same Germanic kling root underlies English clink. [wiktionary]

butterbrot.context_phrase: Ich nehme ein Butterbrot mit in die Schule.
butterbrot.context_translation: I take a sandwich to school.
butterbrot.etymology_derivation: Butter + Brot — both elements are documented twins (Butter via Latin butyrum, Brot kin to brew); an exact internal calque. [wiktionary]

marmelade.etymology_derivation: Marmelade — 16th century, from Middle French marmelade, from Portuguese marmelada (quince jam); English marmalade took the same route. [wiktionary]

pilot.etymology_derivation: Borrowed about 1500 from Italian pilota, partly via French pilote - the same Italian word that gave English pilot. [wiktionary][etymonline]

etage.context_phrase: Wir wohnen in der dritten Etage.
etage.context_translation: We live on the third floor.
etage.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French étage; English stage is a doublet from the same Old French word estage. [wiktionary]

bunt.etymology_derivation: Probably from Latin punctus, a relative of English point — no English color-word cognate; memorize this one. [wiktionary]

französisch.etymology_derivation: From Old French francois plus the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; both trace back to the Franks, whence also English frank. [wiktionary]

englisch.etymology_derivation: From England plus the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the page itself names English English as the cognate, so this is the same word. [wiktionary]

spanisch.etymology_derivation: Spanien + the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the same word as English Spanish. [wiktionary]

pass.etymology_derivation: From Old French pas, from Latin passus (step); the passport sense is a shortening of French passeport, the same source English used. [wiktionary]

gepäck.context_phrase: Mein Gepäck ist noch nicht da.
gepäck.context_translation: My luggage is not here yet.
gepäck.etymology_derivation: A collective of Pack (bundle) — the Low German packing word English also took as pack. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
